title: RMS, peak, peak-to-peak and PEP
idea: One sine wave, three ways to measure its height. RMS is the one that heats a load like DC, so power always uses RMS.

lines: PEP = RMS² / R, with RMS taken at the envelope's peak
Steady, unmodulated carrier: PEP = average power (ratio 1.00)

compare.how: Center line to the top of the wave.
Bottom to top: twice the peak.
0.707 of the peak. The DC voltage that would heat the load the same.
Power at the highest point of the envelope. The FCC limits are in PEP output.

traps.why: That's the peak (120 x 1.414). Peak-to-peak is twice it: 339.4 V.
That's half the peak. RMS is 17 x 0.707 = 12 V.
Peak-to-peak can't go straight into the power formula. Halve it to 250 V peak, x 0.707 = 176.8 V RMS, then 176.8² / 50 = 625 W.
The peak is higher than the DC that would heat the resistor the same. That DC-equivalent value is RMS.
1.414 is the peak-to-RMS voltage factor. A steady carrier's power at its peak equals its average: 1.00.
No doubling: an unmodulated carrier never changes, so PEP equals the average power, 1060 W.
The power rules are written in PEP output from the transmitter.
